exclusions.B: The council should have taken them down the year the county's rule arrived and put up letters that a stranger can read at a glance, instead of waiting for an ambulance to prove the point.
exclusions.C: A street sign has one job, and Marrow's boards did it badly.
exclusions.D: The driver mistook Lower Gate for it, as though the two boards had been swapped, and reached the house eleven minutes late.

support: A street sign has one job, and Marrow's boards did it badly.
Half the boards in town were rotting at the edges, and the Gates, among the first Marrow painted, had faded to grey on cream.
WV12-P01.5.note: The author flatly judges the boards illegible and wishes they had come down years earlier, with no nostalgia for them; the signs are already replaced, so there is nothing left to worry about.

support: Thirty years of rain had beaten on those roofs, and the cedar beneath was still as dry and square as the day she cut it.
I have built six hives of my own since, all to her pattern, and the best of them is a shade less square than either of hers.
WV12-P02.5.note: The narrator dwells on the hives' craftsmanship and durability and copies their pattern while conceding they fall short of it; the hives and keeper are still present, so nothing is lost to be wistful about.

exclusions.A: Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds, as he expects it to next year.
exclusions.B: The council should have paid for lime mortar matched to the old brick, which stays rough enough for a swift to grip.
exclusions.D: The result is a poor repair, a stripe of grey cement from the crack to the chimney's top, so smooth that a swift's claws slide straight off it.
exclusions.E: The council kept the chimney standing, since having it pulled down would have meant scaffolding the whole roof.

support: The council should have paid for lime mortar matched to the old brick, which stays rough enough for a swift to grip.
The birds keep clear of that stripe and crowd into the old brick below it.
WV12-P04.5.note: The writer values the old brick as a roost and wants it restored, but never praises the chimney outright; the passage's only open judgment is disapproval ('a poor repair'), aimed at the council's cement stripe, which is now part of the chimney, so a careful reader could defend B, and admiration is only weakly licensed.
